summary:
How Israeli turnout works, and what it means for a locality "turnout potential" index.

1. National turnout barely moves; Arab turnout drives the swings. Since 2013 national turnout has stayed between 67% and 72%. Over the same period Arab-locality turnout ranged from 44.6% (2021) to 64.8% (2020). In the official CEC locality files, the median Arab locality's turnout moved by about 22 points between 2019 and 2022. The median Jewish or haredi locality moved by about 4.5 points. Turnout potential is therefore mostly an Arab and Druze question. Among Jewish localities it matters only in development towns, low-SES areas and Russian-speaking (FSU) cities.

2. Raw CEC locality turnout is a biased measure. Two corrections are required.
- **Double-envelope votes:** 462,807 in 2022, equal to 6.8% of eligible voters (mostly soldiers). The CEC publishes them only nationally. Adding them back changes turnout very unevenly: +10 points in Judea and Samaria, about +7 in the Centre and Jerusalem, and only about +3 in Arab localities. Without this correction, settlements, high-SES towns and towns with many young people look like they have spare turnout when they do not.
- **Israelis living abroad:** they stay on the voter roll and have no absentee vote. Estimates run from 400,000–500,000 (2013) to about 600,000 (CBS 2016). Emigration surged in 2023–2025 (about 90,000 departures a year), so the 2026 roll probably holds more of these voters, plausibly concentrated in secular, high-SES and FSU localities. Low raw turnout in such places partly reflects people who no longer live there, not voters who can be mobilised.

3. What predicts locality turnout. Atmor, Friedberg and Harsgor's envelope-adjusted 2022 regressions are the best available baseline.
- Jewish localities: SES raises turnout by about 0.5 points per CBS cluster. Development towns are about 6 points lower and kibbutzim about 4 points lower. Settlements are about 5 points higher, and haredi share adds turnout. Distance from the centre has no effect.
- Arab localities: SES matters more (about 1.8 points per cluster). Being closer to the centre adds about 2.2 points per periphery-index unit, and larger towns vote more.
- Residuals from these regressions are a defensible definition of "underperformance".

4. Arab turnout depends on:
- party configuration: unity used to raise turnout, but 2022 broke that rule;
- perceived influence: Odeh's 2019 coalition signal and the 77% who now back an Arab party joining a coalition;
- backlash against delegitimisation: the 2019 polling-station cameras, and possibly the 2026 disqualification fight;
- local candidates: the southern Triangle reached 60.8% versus 46.2% in the northern Triangle;
- polling-station access in the Negev: about 40,000 voters in unrecognised villages are assigned to stations 5–65 km away, and tribal stations had 38% turnout;
- clan (hamula) networks, which matter far more in local elections.

2026 surveys put Arab turnout at about 53% if the parties ran separately and 61–67% under a full Joint List. The actual line-up is a partial reunion (Joint List plus Ra'am running separately), which implies roughly 55–60%. Self-reported intention overstates turnout by 10–40 points and should not be used raw.

5. Haredi localities are already near their ceiling (76–84% raw turnout, almost no movement between elections), so there is no upside there. Druze turnout has fallen to about 49%, yet about 90% of Druze votes go to Zionist parties. That makes Druze localities a real mobilisation pool, and Druze candidates on the list are the main lever.

6. Election-day logistics. Election day is a statutory holiday. Since 2019 intercity buses and trains have been free to everyone; in 2026 this covers intercity lines over 15 km and all trains, but not urban lines. People must vote at the polling station of their registered address, which is a burden for students and young adults living away from home.

7. I found no randomised GOTV studies from Israel. The only evidence is quasi-experimental and confounded: transport drives in the Negev in 2019 coincided with Bedouin-town turnout gains of 10–24 points. For effect sizes, the model should rely on the international literature.

findings.claim: Knesset turnout was very high in the state's first decades: 86.9% in 1949, low 80s from 1955 to 1969, and roughly 77-80% from 1973 to 1999. It fell sharply after the end of direct PM elections, to the mid-60s in 2006-2009, then partly recovered (72.3% in 2015). Caution: this compilation gives 63.9% for 2013 and 68.9% for 2003, which appear to use valid votes; the CEC/IDI figures are 67.8% for both years.
findings.authors: Jewish Virtual Library (compiled from CEC)
findings.title: Voter Turnout in Knesset Elections
findings.relevance: Context only. Today's ceiling sits about 8-10 points below the pre-2000 norm. A 'maximum achievable' turnout of about 78-80% for Jewish non-haredi localities is historically plausible but unlikely in 2026.

findings.claim: Arab and Druze turnout fell from 75% in 1999 to the mid-50s by 2006-2013. It then swung widely: up when the Arab parties ran united (2015, Sep 2019, 2020) and down when they split (Apr 2019, 2021). The gap to national turnout ranged from about 7 to 23 points. Arab localities held 938,401 eligible voters in 2022.
findings.authors: Arik Rudnitzky
findings.title: Summary of the 25th Knesset election results in Arab society (Bayan, Issue 28)
findings.venue: Konrad Adenauer Program for Jewish-Arab Cooperation, Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Shows Arab localities carry almost all the turnout volatility. In the index, give Arab localities a sector-level swing scenario (44-65% historical range) plus locality deviations.

findings.claim: Double-envelope ballots rose from 5.55% of all ballots in Apr 2019 to 9.59% in 2021. They are cast by soldiers away from home (the largest group), hospital patients and staff, prisoners, diplomats, residents of senior-care facilities, and voters using accessible stations. The CEC counts them centrally, so they do not appear in polling-station or locality turnout.
findings.authors: Or Anabi, Ofer Kenig; 2022 figure from Atmor, Friedberg, Harsgor (CEC data)
findings.title: Will the Election Results Hinge on the Double-Envelope Ballots?
findings.relevance: Every locality turnout figure from CEC files must be corrected upward by about 6.8 points of eligible on average, and the correction is not uniform (see D2-F04).

findings.claim: After winning a petition, Atmor, Friedberg and Harsgor obtained the 2022 double envelopes assigned to each of the 1,215 localities. Adding them back raises district turnout very unevenly: by 10 points in Judea and Samaria, about 7-8 points in the Centre, Jerusalem and the South, and about 6 points in Tel Aviv, Haifa and the North. Envelopes equal 7.5% of eligible voters in Jewish and mixed localities but only 2.9% in Arab localities.
findings.quant: Without -> with envelopes: J&S 75.3->85.3; Centre 68.7->75.6; Jerusalem 63.3->71.2; South 62.2->69.3; Tel Aviv 63.4->69.7; North 59.4->65.6; Haifa 59.0->65.3; national 63.8->70.6. Jewish/mixed localities 73.0% vs Arab 56.0% (envelopes included). Eilat 53.6%; Arab Golan localities 27.5%
findings.authors: Liran Harsgor, Chen Friedberg, Nir Atmor
findings.title: Who Flocked to the Polls? Voter Turnout in the 2022 Elections (Hebrew edition, pp. 115-148; English edition DOI 10.4324/9781032633299-5)
findings.venue: The Elections in Israel 2022 (eds. Rahat, Gidron, Shamir), Israel Democracy Institute / Routledge
findings.relevance: Critical for the index. Without the correction, settlements, young-family suburbs and the periphery look about 3-7 points more 'mobilisable' than Arab towns really are. Use sector-specific envelope add-backs or request the authors' locality file.

findings.claim: Jewish and mixed localities (N=1,069): turnout rises with SES and falls in development towns, kibbutzim and larger localities. It is higher in settlements and with higher haredi share. Distance from the centre is not significant once SES is controlled. Arab localities (N=146): SES, proximity to the centre and larger size all raise turnout. In the pooled model, being an Arab locality cuts predicted turnout by 26 points.
findings.quant: Jewish/mixed model: SES +0.53 pts per CBS cluster; development town -6.3; kibbutz -4.3; J&S +4.9; haredi share +0.057 pts per pct-pt (table value; text says 0.57); size -0.73 per normalised unit; adj R2 0.16. Arab model: SES +1.81/cluster; centrality +2.22 per periphery-index unit; size +1.75; adj R2 0.16. Pooled: Arab -26.3; adj R2 0.60
findings.authors: Liran Harsgor, Chen Friedberg, Nir Atmor
findings.title: Who Flocked to the Polls? Voter Turnout in the 2022 Elections
findings.venue: The Elections in Israel 2022, IDI (Hebrew) / Routledge (English)
findings.relevance: Use as the 'expected turnout' baseline. Turnout potential = expected (or historical-maximum) turnout minus actual envelope-adjusted turnout, so a development town scoring below even its conditional prediction ranks high.

findings.claim: Among Jewish and mixed localities, the gap between peripheral and central localities is small but widened from 2.5 points (Apr 2019) to 3.6 (Sep 2019) to 4.4 (2022). Among Arab localities the gaps are far larger and swing from election to election. Peripheral Arab localities ranged from 38.7% (2019a) to 52.4% (2020); central Arab localities from 54.5% (2021) to 75.6% (2020). Figures exclude envelopes.
findings.quant: Jewish periphery-centre gap: 2.5 / 3.6 / 4.4 pts. Arab gap: 25.7 (2019a), 14.2 (2021), 19.6 (2022). Arab peripheral max 52.4% vs central max 75.6%
findings.authors: Liran Harsgor, Chen Friedberg, Nir Atmor
findings.title: Who Flocked to the Polls? Voter Turnout in the 2022 Elections
findings.relevance: Sets ceilings. Central Arab localities have reached about 75%, so a 'potential' near 70-75% is realistic for Arab towns. The biggest headroom is in peripheral (Negev, Golan) Arab localities.

findings.topic: Arab turnout determinants: unity, choice, threshold, boycott
findings.claim: In every election from 2013 to 2021, Arab turnout rose only when the Arab parties ran united. In 2022 turnout rose despite a three-way split. Rudnitzky's explanations: voters had distinct options, people who abstained in 2021 found a list to vote for, boycott declarations were reversed, and many voted tactically to push Balad over the threshold. He estimates Balad would have passed at 60% Arab turnout. The unity effect is real but depends on context.
findings.quant: 2021 44.6% -> 2022 53.2% with three separate lists; Arab lists won 85.8% of Arab votes; Ra'am 35.2%, Hadash-Ta'al 28.8%, Balad 21.8%; Arab votes for Jewish parties 14.2%
findings.authors: Arik Rudnitzky
findings.title: Summary of the 25th Knesset election results in Arab society (Bayan 28); also IDI analyses of 9 Nov and 25 Dec 2022
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center / Israel Democracy Institute
findings.relevance: The 2026 line-up (Joint List of Hadash-Ta'al-Balad, with Ra'am separate) is a partial reunion, which supports a central Arab turnout of about 55-60%. Threshold anxiety for Ra'am, plus Balad voters left without their leader, adds uncertainty.

findings.topic: Arab turnout by region and locality (2022); local-candidate effect
findings.claim: Arab turnout in 2022 varied widely by sub-region and town. The southern Triangle (home towns of top candidates Walid Taha and Ahmad Tibi) reached 60.8%; the northern Triangle reached only 46.2%. Several large towns stayed below 50%. Rudnitzky attributes much of the variation to a 'local candidate' effect.
findings.quant: North 53.9% (573,878 eligible); Triangle 52.5% (211,980); Negev 51.0% (144,860); Jerusalem corridor 55.9%. High: Jaljulya 69.5, Sakhnin 68.4, Kafr Qassem 66.9, Majd al-Kurum 66.7, Kafr Manda 65.2, Kafr Bara 64.8, Tamra 63.5, Tira 62.3. Low: Umm al-Fahm 38.3, Maghar 44.0, Baqa al-Gharbiyye 47.5, Nazareth 48.3, Shefa-'Amr 51.5
findings.authors: Arik Rudnitzky
findings.title: Analysis of Arab voting in the 25th Knesset elections
findings.relevance: Large low-turnout Arab cities (Umm al-Fahm, Nazareth, Baqa, Shefa-'Amr) are the biggest absolute vote reservoirs. Candidate home towns behave differently, so check 2026 slates for local candidates when scoring.

findings.claim: About 40,000 Bedouin voters in unrecognised Negev villages have no polling station in their village. They are assigned by tribe to stations 5-65 km away, which can mean 1-2 hours each way without a car. Turnout at tribal stations has always been far below recognised Bedouin towns. A 2022 petition for stations in village service centres was rejected. Ra'am took about 74-75% of the Negev Bedouin vote in 2022.
findings.quant: Tribal stations: 24.6% (2009), 34.2% (2015), 42.1% (Sep 2019), 32.4% (2021), 38% (2022). Recognised Bedouin communities: 35.9%, 47.0%, 52.1%, 45.8%, 56% (same years). INSS 2022: townships incl. Rahat ~60%, regional councils ~57%, unrecognised villages <40%
findings.authors: The Abraham Initiatives; Lavie, Wattad, Abu Gweder, Shahbari, Essa, Elran (INSS Insight 1661)
findings.title: Ensuring Access to the Right to Vote for the Knesset among Residents of the Unrecognized Bedouin Villages in the Negev (policy paper, 18 Jan 2024); Arab Society in Israel and the Elections to the 25th Knesset (INSS, 20 Nov 2022)
findings.relevance: Distance is the binding constraint, so this is where transport programmes work best. Higher Negev turnout mainly helps Ra'am clear the threshold, which matters for the 19% change-bloc-plus-Ra'am path. Score these localities on turnout potential, with transport as the tactic and bloc impact routed through Ra'am.

findings.claim: Zazim ran 50 minibuses that took about 5,000 Bedouin voters from unrecognised villages to polling stations in April 2019, despite a Likud petition to stop it. In September 2019, after another Likud challenge, about 300 volunteers drove voters in their own cars. In the official CEC files, Negev Bedouin towns gained 10-24 points between Apr and Sep 2019, more than the Arab average of about +11. Joint List reunification is a confound.
findings.quant: Zazim Apr 2019: 50 minibuses, ~5,000 voters. CEC regular-kalpi turnout 2019a->2019s: Tel Sheva 30.9->54.9; Laqiya 22.9->46.3; Hura 29.2->45.1; Kuseife 41.3->58.6; Rahat 49.6->59.5. Tribal stations ~20% (Apr 2019, per Adalah) -> 42.1% (Sep 2019)
findings.authors: Zazim; Mohammad Darawshe (Bayan, Moshe Dayan Center)
findings.title: Moving forward together (Zazim, 22 May 2019); The Spring's Back in their Steps: Arab Politics Following the Twenty-second Knesset Elections (27 Nov 2019)
findings.relevance: Suggestive (not causal) evidence that transport-constrained Bedouin localities respond strongly. The index should give extra elasticity to localities with known access barriers.

findings.claim: Druze turnout has fallen for three decades, from about 77-79% in 1996-1999 to the mid-50s by 2015-2019, and averaged 48.7% in 2021-2022. Explanations include alienation after the 2018 Nation-State Law, weakening family-based vote brokering, and neglect of the periphery. Druze voters strongly reward Druze candidates in realistic slots (Meretz won 64.8% in Beit Jann in Apr 2019 with a local Druze candidate). About 90% of Druze votes go to Zionist parties.
findings.authors: Omri Eilat & Mahmoud Shanan; Salim Brake; Arik Rudnitzky
findings.title: Community, Society and Trends: Druze Voting Patterns in Knesset Elections 1996-2020 (Bayan, 18 Mar 2021); The Druze Vote in the 20th-22nd Knesset Elections (Bayan, 27 Nov 2019)
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Druze localities (Daliyat al-Karmel, Yarka, Beit Jann, Maghar, Isfiya, Julis, Hurfeish) combine low turnout with Zionist voting, so they are a high-value target for Yashar, YB and Together. Druze candidates on the slate and Nation-State Law messaging are the levers.

findings.claim: Haredi localities vote at very high and stable rates. UTJ's vote has grown about 3.95% a year from 1992 to 2022, close to the growth of the haredi Ashkenazi adult population (about 4.1% a year after mortality). Malach therefore concludes UTJ already mobilises about 95% of its potential electorate. Haredi municipal turnout also held steady between 2018 and 2024.
findings.quant: CEC raw regular-kalpi 2022: Bnei Brak 76.5%, Modiin Illit 82.0%, Beitar Illit 81.3%, Elad 84.4%. Haredi sector turnout range across 2019-2022 ~4.6 pts. UTJ voter growth 3.95%/yr vs eligible growth 4.1-4.3%/yr; shortfall ~12,000 votes over 30 years
findings.authors: Gilad Malach
findings.title: Does the growth of United Torah Judaism match the growth of the haredi population? (chapter in The Elections in Israel 2022, Hebrew edition, pp. 371ff)
findings.relevance: Haredi localities get roughly zero turnout potential. Their demographic growth adds a mechanical tailwind to the Netanyahu bloc each cycle, which raises the turnout the change bloc needs elsewhere.

findings.topic: Who abstains: SES, age, FSU immigrants (survey + locality data)
findings.claim: In 2013, turnout ran from about 57% in CBS clusters 1-2 to 74.5% in clusters 8-10. Non-haredi Jewish localities in the lowest clusters voted at only about 52%. In surveys, voters aged 18-22, Arabs, lower-class respondents and FSU immigrants reported the most abstention. About half of those who said beforehand they would not vote ended up voting. IDI estimated true 2013 turnout among residents at about 75%, against 67.8% official.
findings.quant: 2013: clusters 1-2 56.7%, 8-10 74.5%, non-haredi Jewish clusters 1-2 51.6%. Post-election reported non-voting: age 18-22 14.9%, Arabs 18.1%, FSU immigrants 15.7%, lower class 16.0%, Jews overall 6.8%, haredim 1.4%
findings.authors: Ella Heller
findings.title: Who Doesn't Vote in the Israeli Knesset Elections?
findings.relevance: Supports weighting low-SES non-haredi Jewish localities and FSU-heavy cities as Jewish-sector turnout targets. These are partly YB and Likud swing territory.

findings.claim: Israel has no absentee voting except for diplomats and emissaries, but citizens living abroad generally stay on the voter roll, so official turnout understates turnout among residents. INSS (Yehuda Ben Meir) estimated 400,000-500,000 registered voters abroad in 2013. Removing them lifts 2013 turnout from 67.8% to about 73%, and Jewish turnout to about 75%. CBS estimated 560,000-596,000 Israelis abroad at end-2016 (not counting children born abroad).
findings.quant: Abroad registrants ~400-500k in 2013 (~7-9% of a 5.66m roll); adjusted 2013 turnout 73% (Jews 75%) vs 67.8% official; CBS end-2016 560-596k Israelis abroad
findings.authors: Yehuda Ben Meir (INSS), reported by JNS/Algemeiner; CBS via press
findings.title: Israeli Population Analysis Reveals Higher Voter Turnout Than Initial Reports
findings.relevance: The index's denominator should be resident voters. Subtracting an abroad share (about 7-9% nationally, higher where emigration is concentrated) prevents low raw turnout in emigrant-heavy localities from being read as mobilisable slack.

findings.claim: A Tel Aviv University study using CBS data counted 268,930 Israelis who left for 3+ consecutive months in 2023-2025, against 83,219 in 2013-2015. The authors estimate 45,000-50,000 of 2025's leavers will stay abroad 12+ months. The study gives no breakdown by locality.
findings.authors: Itai Ater, Netai Bergman, Doron Zamir (TAU)
findings.title: Study of emigration from Israel 2023-2025 (reported 3 Aug 2026)
findings.relevance: The 2026 roll probably holds more people living abroad than 2022's did, plausibly concentrated in secular, high-SES and tech-heavy central localities (the change bloc's strongholds). Raise the abroad-adjustment there, and do not chase apparent 'turnout potential' that is really people who have emigrated. (Locality concentration is an inference.)

findings.topic: Expat voting in 2026: Code 51 and Fly&Vote
findings.claim: Citizens the state classifies as non-residents (Code 51) are removed from the voter roll. A petition by expats who found they had been removed was dismissed by the High Court on procedural grounds. The AID Coalition's Fly&Vote had about 31,000 registrants by August 2026 and aims for 70,000. It does not pay for flights, though some 'scholarships' may be available. Likud calls the scheme an electoral bribe. Returning expats must vote at their home polling station.
findings.quant: ~31,000 registered (Aug 2026), target 70,000; AID survey: 45% of Israelis abroad would make every effort to vote; no official count of Code 51 removals
findings.authors: eJewishPhilanthropy; Times of Israel / JTA reporting
findings.title: Inside the effort to bring tens of thousands of expats to Israel to vote
findings.relevance: Scenario input: 20-70k extra votes (about 0.4-1.4% of turnout) landing in the home towns of emigrants, mostly secular central localities. Do not build targeting around it; it is legally and politically contested.

findings.topic: Election-day logistics: holiday, hours, free intercity transit
findings.claim: Election day is a statutory holiday, and most polling stations open 07:00-22:00 (08:00-20:00 in small communities). Since April 2019, intercity buses and trains have been free to all from 20:00 on election eve until service ends. Before that, only voters registered more than 20 km from their station could get a free ticket, and only by advance registration. For 27 Oct 2026 the CEC made intercity lines over 15 km and all trains free; urban lines are not covered, and Eilat requires registration.
findings.quant: Pre-2019 scheme cost NIS 2.4m; 2019 universal scheme ~NIS 3m; 2026: intercity >15 km + all trains free from 20:00 on 26 Oct
findings.authors: Calcalist Tech; The Jerusalem Post; Central Elections Committee
findings.title: Israel to Offer Free Inter-City Rides on Election Day (2019); free transport for 27 Oct 2026 (JPost, 20 Sep 2026); CEC Guide to Knesset Elections (2022)
findings.relevance: Lowers the travel cost for students and young adults registered at their parents' address, so the residual barrier is mostly intra-city and rural transport (Arab towns, Negev). Campaign-funded local transport has its highest value where public transit is weak.

findings.claim: Voters may vote only at the polling station assigned to their registered address. Exceptions use double envelopes (soldiers, hospitalised people, prisoners, women in shelters, diplomats, people with mobility impairments at accessible stations). A 2016 CEC recommendation to let voters use another station after notifying the registry was welcomed by IDI's Ofer Kenig, but the 2022 guide still had the strict rule.
findings.quant: Registration cut-off for 2022: entered in the Population Registry by 8 Sep 2022 (~54 days before the vote)
findings.authors: Central Elections Committee; Israel Democracy Institute (Ofer Kenig)
findings.title: Guide to Knesset Elections (25th Knesset); IDI Scholar Applauds Efforts to Expand From Where Israelis Can Cast Their Ballots (23 Jun 2016)
findings.relevance: Locality turnout is the turnout of registered residents, not people actually living there. Targeting lists should go by registered address. Young-adult GOTV needs reminders to travel to the parents' town; periphery towns with many young people studying or working in the centre show 'potential' that needs travel nudges, not local canvassing.

findings.claim: Surveys by the Konrad Adenauer Program put expected Arab turnout around 52-53% if the four Arab parties run separately, and 62-67% if the full four-party Joint List were rebuilt. Crime and personal security dominate concerns, and over three-quarters back an Arab party joining the next coalition.
findings.quant: Nov 2025: 52.4% separate / 61.8% united (15.5 seats); May 2026: 53% separate / 67% united (16.3 seats); separate-run seats May 2026: Hadash-Ta'al 5.3, Ra'am 4.6, Balad 1.8. 76.9% weak personal security; 77.2% support Arab party in coalition (43.3% any government, 33.9% centre-left)
findings.authors: Arik Rudnitzky (Konrad Adenauer Program, Moshe Dayan Center)
findings.title: Integration and Influence: Survey of Arab Citizens in Israel (14 May 2026); In-depth survey following the Israel-Hamas ceasefire (25 Nov 2025)
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Anchors the 2026 Arab sector turnout scenario. The actual line-up (Joint List of three parties plus Ra'am) sits between the two scenarios, at about 55-60%. Perceived coalition influence motivates these voters, so change-bloc signalling on cooperation matters.

findings.topic: Young Arab voters, women, and GOTV messaging (2026)
findings.claim: An Abraham Initiatives survey of young Arab citizens (Feb 2026, n=614) put expected turnout at 58.8-61.9%. Respondents want concrete plans on crime, housing, jobs and discrimination rather than vague talk of partnership. The ACI Task Force (Aug 2026) reports about 59% expected turnout among Arab 18-34s. Arab women are less likely than men to say they will 'definitely' vote, and the Task Force calls women and youth the largest sources of potential turnout growth.
findings.quant: Young Arab expected turnout 58.8-61.9% (Feb 2026); 18-34 ~59% (ACI, source unattributed); Statnet/Abraham: 30% cite lack of political impact and 18% internal Arab division as reasons for not voting
findings.authors: The Abraham Initiatives; Task Force on Arab Citizens of Israel
findings.title: Young Arab Voter Survey (14 Aug 2026); Arab Society and Israel's 2026 Elections: Between Electoral Power and Political Influence (12 Aug 2026)
findings.venue: The Abraham Initiatives / ACI Task Force
findings.relevance: Arab GOTV content should be concrete on crime and services. Target women and young people inside high-potential Arab localities, and give extra weight to localities with large youth cohorts.

findings.topic: Self-report bias: calibration for turnout polls
findings.claim: Surveys badly overstate Arab turnout. In ArPanel's January 2026 poll, 66% said they voted in the last election (actual 53.2%). In IDI's Aug-Sep 2026 Israeli Voice Index, only 8.7% of Arab respondents said they don't intend to vote, against about 47% who abstained in 2022 (Jews 1.2%). Modelled pre-election estimates also miss: KAP's 49% forecast in Oct 2022 versus 53.2% actual, and Abraham Initiatives' 56% in Mar 2019 versus 49.2% actual. The same Voice Index found crime in Arab society was the top voting consideration for 31.5% of Arab respondents.
findings.quant: Recall overstatement ~13 pts (66% vs 53.2%); stated non-intention 8.7% vs ~47% actual non-voting; modelled forecast errors +4.2 and -6.8 pts
findings.authors: ArPanel (via Jerusalem Post); Viterbi Center, Israel Democracy Institute; Konrad Adenauer Program; Abraham Initiatives
findings.title: Supermajority of Israeli Arabs support re-establishing Joint List (JPost, 6 Feb 2026); The Israeli Voice Index - August 2026 (data file)
findings.relevance: Do not feed raw intention-to-vote into the index. Use modelled estimates with about ±6-point error and anchor on the official CEC history.

findings.topic: Turnout volatility by sector (official CEC locality data)
findings.claim: Our own calculation from the official CEC locality files (2019a-2022; localities with ≥1,000 eligible voters; regular polling stations only, excluding envelopes) shows Arab-majority localities are about five times as volatile as Jewish or haredi localities. Each Arab locality also moves around its sector's swing with a standard deviation of about 6 points.
findings.quant: Weighted turnout, Arab-majority (n=98): 48.7, 60.1, 66.2, 44.6, 53.9; haredi (n=10): 76.3, 76.8, 76.6, 72.8, 75.8; other Jewish (n=227): 65.6, 64.9, 65.2, 62.0, 64.0. Median locality max-min range: Arab 22.1 pts, haredi 4.6, Jewish 4.5. SD of locality deviation from sector swing: Arab 6.0, Jewish 3.4, haredi 1.3. Arab sector swings: +12.3, +5.7, -19.8, +8.6 pts
findings.authors: Desk 2 calculation from Central Elections Committee official results
findings.title: Sector turnout volatility, Knesset elections 2019-2022 (computed)
findings.venue: CEC official locality results (project file data/processed/kalpi_localities.parquet)
findings.relevance: Direct elasticity parameters: a turnout-potential score should scale headroom by observed swing range. Arab localities have real, demonstrated elasticity; Jewish localities rarely move more than 3-4 points. (URL points to the IDI volume that reproduces the CEC data; the numbers themselves are our calculation from the project's CEC file.)

findings.topic: Clan (hamula) mobilisation and local vs national elections
findings.claim: Studies cited by Atmor, Friedberg and Harsgor (Ben-Bassat and Dahan 2012) find hamula structure strongly drives Arab turnout as a mobilising force. That is why Arab turnout in local elections, where clan ties matter more, is far higher than in Knesset elections. In the Feb 2024 local elections, Arab-locality turnout fell 10 points from 2018, versus 4.5 points in non-haredi Jewish localities and 0.5 in haredi ones.
findings.quant: Local turnout change 2018->2024: Arab -10 pts; non-haredi Jewish -4.5; haredi -0.5
findings.authors: Ariel Finkelstein (IDI); Harsgor, Friedberg, Atmor citing Ben-Bassat & Dahan (2012)
findings.title: Analysis of the 2024 Local Elections (17 Apr 2024)
findings.relevance: Arab localities have latent mobilisation capacity through clan and local-leader networks. Partnering with local leaders (mayors, clan heads) is the realistic way to reach it. Arab disengagement deepened in 2024, so the baseline is fragile.

findings.claim: Darawshe attributes the Sep 2019 Arab turnout jump (49% to 59%) partly to backlash against Netanyahu's anti-Arab campaigning, including the threat to put cameras in polling stations, and to Odeh's statement that he would back a centre-left government. In 2026 the CEC voted to bar the Joint List, Ra'am and MK Cassif. The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the ban on both lists on 2 Oct 2026 and reversed Cassif's 7-2; Balad leader Abu Shehadeh withdrew before the ruling. The ACI Task Force warns that framing the opposition as dependent on Arab parties can deepen alienation.
findings.quant: Arab turnout Apr 2019 49% -> Sep 2019 59%; 2026 Supreme Court: Joint List and Ra'am bans overturned unanimously, Cassif 7-2
findings.authors: Mohammad Darawshe (Dayan Center); Times of Israel
findings.title: Supreme Court unanimously overturns election panel's ban on Arab parties (2 Oct 2026)
findings.relevance: A possible upside risk to Arab turnout in 2026, which argues for widening the Arab scenario band upward. For messaging, change-bloc communications should avoid treating Arab votes as illegitimate.

findings.topic: Civil-society GOTV infrastructure in Arab society
findings.claim: Before Sep 2019, Coalition 17/9 (11 organisations, hundreds of volunteers) targeted 25 Arab towns with especially low turnout. It used canvassing at churches and mosques, help finding polling stations, Arabic leaflets, billboards and social media; its internal poll projected 56% turnout, and actual turnout was 59%. In 2022 a coalition including the Arab Center for Alternative Planning, Ajyal and Standing Together ran field work, billboards and influencer videos in the Negev, Galilee and Triangle. No rigorous evaluation of any of these exists.
findings.quant: 25 targeted low-turnout towns (2019); 11 member organisations; pre-2022 polls predicted 40-50% Arab turnout vs 53.2% actual
findings.authors: The Abraham Initiatives (reprint of Times of Israel report); Al-Monitor
findings.title: Inside the grassroots drive to get Israel's Arabs to vote (27 Aug 2019); Arab groups cooperate to raise turnout in Israeli election (Oct 2022)
findings.relevance: Organised GOTV networks already exist and target by low turnout, which is the same logic as our index. The campaign playbook should coordinate with or support these networks rather than duplicate them. Effect sizes must come from international experiments (other desks).

findings.claim: An IDI survey of 18-22-year-old first-time voters (May 2026; Jewish n=422, Arab n=154) found 80-95% across groups think or are sure they will vote. About 72% of secular Jewish youth were 'sure', the highest certainty among Jewish groups. 87% of Arab youth said they intend to vote, and haredi youth reported the most political interest (77%). Press estimates put the first-time cohort at about 550,000-640,000 (not verified against CBS).
findings.quant: 80-95% think/sure will vote; secular 72% sure; Arab youth 87% intend; ±4.08% margin. Sample weighted 35% secular, 19.5% haredi, 18% religious, 27.5% traditional
findings.authors: Tami Hoffman, Mital Baron (IDI)
findings.title: Survey of first-time voters ahead of the 26th Knesset elections (17 Jun 2026)
findings.relevance: Intentions are heavily overstated (see D2-F21), but the ranking is informative: secular youth are motivated yet face the home-polling-station travel burden. Youth-heavy localities (haredi, settler, Arab) are where cohort growth changes the base.

findings.topic: Development towns and FSU-heavy cities: low raw turnout
findings.claim: Holding SES and geography constant, development towns vote about 6.3 points less than other Jewish localities. Raw regular-station turnout in 2022 was especially low in FSU-heavy and older coastal or northern cities, and higher in development towns with large religious or haredi populations. Part of the FSU-city gap likely reflects people who emigrated and elderly residents, not mobilisable abstainers.
findings.quant: CEC raw 2022 (excluding envelopes): Bat Yam 50.8, Nof HaGalil 52.8, Haifa 55.5, Kiryat Yam 55.6, Karmiel 57.1, Kiryat Shmona 61.1, Ashkelon 61.9, Beersheba 61.3, Dimona 63.6, Ashdod 64.4, Sderot 65.6, Ofakim 68.6, Netivot 75.5 vs Hod HaSharon 74.4, Shoham 76.0
findings.authors: Harsgor, Friedberg, Atmor (coefficients); Desk 2 calculation from CEC official results
findings.title: Who Flocked to the Polls? Voter Turnout in the 2022 Elections; CEC locality results
findings.venue: The Elections in Israel 2022, IDI; CEC
findings.relevance: FSU-heavy cities are Yisrael Beytenu's base and Likud-YB swing ground. They score high on raw headroom but need an abroad and elderly adjustment before ranking. Development towns are mostly Likud base, so mobilising them helps the other bloc; score turnout potential jointly with expected bloc share.

parameters.name: envelope_addback_pct_of_eligible
parameters.value: National 6.8; Jewish/mixed localities 7.5; Arab localities 2.9; Judea and Samaria 10.0
parameters.basis: D2-F03, D2-F04. Add these to CEC regular-station locality turnout before computing headroom. Without a locality file, impute by sector and district, with settlements and young-family localities at the high end and haredi and Arab localities at the low end.

parameters.name: abroad_share_of_roll_2026
parameters.range: 6-10% nationally; plausibly 10-15% in secular high-SES central cities and FSU-heavy cities, 2-4% in haredi and Arab localities (assumption)
parameters.basis: D2-F14 (400-500k in 2013, about 7-9% of roll; IDI implied about 9.6%), D2-F15 (2023-25 emigration surge), D2-F16. The locality distribution is an inference; treat it as a sensitivity parameter.

parameters.name: resident_turnout_ceiling
parameters.basis: D2-F01 (pre-2000 norm about 78-80%), D2-F06 (central Arab localities reached 75.6% in 2020; Arab 75% in 1999), D2-F12 (haredi saturation), D2-F11 (Druze about 60% as recently as 2019a). Headroom = ceiling - (CEC turnout + envelope add-back) / (1 - abroad share).

parameters.name: arab_sector_turnout_2026_central
parameters.basis: D2-F19 (53% separate / 67% full Joint List; actual line-up is a partial reunion), D2-F20 (young voters 59-62%), D2-F07 (2022 rise despite the split), D2-F24 (possible backlash upside), D2-F21 (forecast errors about ±6).

parameters.name: arab_sector_swing_sd
parameters.basis: D2-F22: Arab sector swings across 2019-2022 were +12.3, +5.7, -19.8, +8.6 points.

parameters.name: turnout_elasticity_multiplier_by_sector
parameters.value: Arab 1.0; Druze 0.8; Bedouin with access barriers 1.2; FSU/development-town 0.35; other Jewish 0.25; haredi 0.05
parameters.range: Relative scaling of how much campaign effort can move turnout
parameters.basis: D2-F22 (median locality range: Arab 22 pts vs Jewish and haredi about 4.5), D2-F10 (transport-constrained Bedouin gained 16-24 pts), D2-F11, D2-F12, D2-F27. Calibrated as ratio of observed swing ranges; judgemental.

parameters.name: expected_turnout_regression_coefficients
parameters.range: Coefficient SEs: SES 0.15 (Jewish), 0.68 (Arab); devtown 1.47; kibbutz 0.56; JS 0.75; Arab centrality 0.97
parameters.basis: D2-F05 (Atmor, Friedberg, Harsgor 2025; envelope-adjusted 2022 turnout). Use residuals as an 'underperformance' component of turnout potential.

parameters.name: negev_tribal_station_turnout_upside
parameters.value: +12 pts achievable with transport and access investment
parameters.basis: D2-F09 (tribal stations 38% in 2022 vs 56% in recognised Bedouin communities), D2-F10 (tribal stations about 20% to 42% between Apr and Sep 2019 alongside volunteer transport).

parameters.name: druze_turnout_baseline_and_candidate_bonus
parameters.value: Baseline 49%; +6 pts with a salient Druze candidate on a change-bloc list
parameters.basis: D2-F11 (2021-22 average 48.7%; 2019a 60.1% with Meretz Druze candidate; Beit Jann 64.8% Meretz).

parameters.name: self_report_discount_arab
parameters.value: Subtract 13 pts from recalled turnout; ignore stated non-intention
parameters.basis: D2-F21 (ArPanel 66% recalled vs 53.2% actual; IDI 8.7% stated non-voters vs about 47% actual).

parameters.name: expat_returnee_votes_2026
parameters.basis: D2-F16 (31,000 registered with Fly&Vote by Aug 2026; target 70,000; not all will travel). Allocate mainly to secular central localities; scenario only.

parameters.name: double_envelope_total_2026
parameters.basis: D2-F03 trend (240k to 463k, 2019-2022); likely more reservists in 2026 (unverified). Affects national turnout reporting and locality add-backs.

open_questions: Locality-level double-envelope counts exist only for 2022 (obtained by Atmor, Friedberg and Harsgor via a CEC petition). Can the team get their file, or file the same petition for 2019-2021, to correct locality turnout properly?

There is no published estimate of abroad registrants by locality. Could CBS emigration-by-last-locality tables, or Interior Ministry Code 51 counts, be used to build a locality abroad-share adjustment? How many people were moved to Code 51 before the 2026 roll closed?

The 2026 registered electorate, number of polling stations and expected double-envelope volume (reservists, evacuees) were not found in official CEC releases. Check the CEC's 26th Knesset data release.

I found no randomised or rigorously evaluated GOTV study from Israel (SMS, canvassing, transport). Israeli evidence is quasi-experimental and confounded, so effect sizes must come from the international literature (other desks).

Arab women's turnout: a press summary of a 2024 Statnet poll put women's expected turnout at 37%, but I could not verify it, so it is excluded. Is there CEC data or a reliable survey on the Arab gender turnout gap?

Will the 2026 disqualification fight (CEC ban reversed by the Supreme Court on 2 Oct; Abu Shehadeh withdrew) and Balad's leadership loss raise or lower Arab turnout? Late-October Arab-sector polls (KAP, Statnet, ArPanel, Afkar) should be tracked.

First-time voters: estimates range from 550,000 to 640,000. Verify against CBS. Also check how many post-2022 immigrants from Russia, Ukraine and Belarus are now eligible, and what their likely turnout is.

I found no study measuring Russian-speaking (FSU) turnout directly after 2015. Low raw turnout in FSU-heavy cities could reflect emigration, age structure or real abstention; this needs polling-station-level analysis of FSU neighbourhoods.

Research limitation: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through this desk. Items above marked medium confidence or 'unverified' (e.g. first-time voter counts, Statnet women figure, 2026 envelope expectations) could not be cross-checked with further searches.
